<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">JavaScript</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">UI</span>
  </div>

  <p>Hey there! Today we're building something almost every image heavy site eventually needs, a real image lightbox, entirely from scratch, no library, no dependency, just plain code you can actually read end to end.</p>

  <p class="bx-lede">Ever clicked a thumbnail and watched a full size photo smoothly fade in over a dark background, arrow keys already working before you even reached for the mouse? That is a javascript lightbox gallery doing its job, and every line building one is below, proven with a real browser rather than described in the abstract.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="javascript-lightbox-gallery-basics-what-it-actually-needs-to-do">JavaScript Lightbox Gallery Basics: What It Actually Needs to Do</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A javascript lightbox gallery is a full screen overlay that shows one image at a time, on top of a dimmed background, with a way to move to the next or previous image and a way to close it entirely.</p>

  <p>That short description hides four real requirements: showing the right image, navigating with the keyboard, keeping the page underneath from scrolling while it is open, and returning focus to wherever the visitor started once it closes. Every one of those is built and proven below.</p>

  <p>A photography portfolio, a product page with multiple angles of the same item, and a blog post with an inline image grid all lean on the exact same javascript lightbox gallery mechanics underneath, only the surrounding page design changes. The core behavior built in this guide transfers directly to all three.</p>

  <p>None of it depends on a framework either. Every code sample below runs against plain DOM elements, so the same approach drops cleanly into a static HTML page, a WordPress theme, or a component inside React or Vue with only minor adjustment.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="navigation-math-wrapping-around-the-gallery">Navigation Math: Wrapping Around the Gallery</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Moving to the next or previous image needs to wrap around cleanly, pressing next on the last image should loop back to the first, not stop dead or throw an error.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">nav.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">nextIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">current</span>, <span class="tok-val">total</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> (<span class="tok-val">current</span> + <span class="tok-val">1</span>) % <span class="tok-val">total</span>;
}

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">prevIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">current</span>, <span class="tok-val">total</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">return</span> (<span class="tok-val">current</span> - <span class="tok-val">1</span> + <span class="tok-val">total</span>) % <span class="tok-val">total</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>The <code>+ total</code> inside <code>prevIndex</code> is the one detail worth pausing on. Without it, going backward from index 0 produces a negative number, and JavaScript's modulo operator does not automatically wrap a negative result back into range the way a lot of other languages behave.</p>

  <p>Testing that edge case specifically matters more than it might seem. A gallery with just two or three images makes wraparound bugs obvious almost immediately, but a gallery with dozens of photos can hide a broken wraparound for a long time, since most visitors browse a handful of images near wherever they started and never actually reach the boundary.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Node.js output proving next and previous navigation both wrap around a 4 image gallery correctly">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from nav.js, run against a real 4 image gallery in both directions.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="preloading-neighbors-so-navigation-feels-instant">Preloading Neighbors So Navigation Feels Instant</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The moment a lightbox opens on an image, it already knows exactly which two images the visitor is most likely to ask for next, whichever image sits on either side of it.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">preload.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">preloadedCache</span> = {};

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">preload</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">preloadedCache</span>[<span class="tok-val">index</span>]) <span class="tok-kw">return</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">const</span> <span class="tok-val">img</span> = <span class="tok-kw">new</span> Image();
  <span class="tok-val">img</span>.src = <span class="tok-val">images</span>[<span class="tok-val">index</span>];
  <span class="tok-val">preloadedCache</span>[<span class="tok-val">index</span>] = <span class="tok-val">img</span>;
}

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">showImage</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>) {
  <span class="tok-val">lightboxImg</span>.src = <span class="tok-val">images</span>[<span class="tok-val">index</span>];
  <span class="tok-fn">preload</span>(<span class="tok-fn">nextIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>, <span class="tok-val">images</span>.length));
  <span class="tok-fn">preload</span>(<span class="tok-fn">prevIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>, <span class="tok-val">images</span>.length));
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Creating a real <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLImageElement/Image" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><code>Image()</code></a> object and setting its <code>src</code> is enough to make the browser fetch and cache that file immediately, even though the object itself is never inserted into the page. This one trick is the entire reason a well built javascript lightbox gallery can feel instant rather than making a visitor wait on every single navigation.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p>Chrome DevTools' <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/network" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Network panel</a> shows every one of these preload requests happening in real time, useful for confirming the cache is actually warm before a visitor ever presses next.</p>
  </div>

  <p>Proving this works needs more than reading the code. Driving a real browser through an open, a navigation, and tracking every real network request that fires shows exactly when each image gets fetched, and whether the preload actually pays off.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real Chromium output proving a preloaded neighbor image is not re-requested when navigated to, and that focus correctly returns to the original thumbnail after closing">
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Real clicks, real keydowns, real network request tracking in Chromium via Playwright.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p>Once a browser has fetched a file, creating a second <code>Image()</code> pointed at the exact same URL does not trigger a new network request at all, it resolves straight from the browser's own HTTP cache, which is the entire mechanism this preloading trick relies on.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="keyboard-navigation-and-locking-background-scroll">Keyboard Navigation and Locking Background Scroll</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A javascript lightbox gallery that only responds to mouse clicks leaves out a real category of visitors. Arrow keys and Escape need to work the moment the overlay opens.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">keyboardNav.js</div>
    <pre><code>document.addEventListener(<span class="tok-str">'keydown'</span>, (<span class="tok-val">e</span>) =&gt; {
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (!<span class="tok-val">lightbox</span>.classList.contains(<span class="tok-str">'open'</span>)) <span class="tok-kw">return</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">e</span>.key === <span class="tok-str">'Escape'</span>) <span class="tok-fn">closeLightbox</span>();
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">e</span>.key === <span class="tok-str">'ArrowRight'</span>) <span class="tok-fn">showImage</span>(<span class="tok-fn">nextIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">currentIndex</span>, <span class="tok-val">images</span>.length));
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">e</span>.key === <span class="tok-str">'ArrowLeft'</span>) <span class="tok-fn">showImage</span>(<span class="tok-fn">prevIndex</span>(<span class="tok-val">currentIndex</span>, <span class="tok-val">images</span>.length));
});</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>The background also needs to stop scrolling while the lightbox is open, otherwise a visitor can accidentally scroll the page underneath a full screen overlay without realizing it, a small detail that feels broken the moment it is missing.</p>

  <p>The fade in transition itself deserves one more consideration: a visitor with <code>prefers-reduced-motion</code> enabled, supported everywhere according to <a href="https://caniuse.com/prefers-reduced-motion" target="_blank" rel="noopener">caniuse.com</a>, should see the lightbox appear instantly rather than animate, since motion sensitivity is a real accessibility need, not a style preference to override by default.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">scrollLock.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">openLightbox</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>, <span class="tok-val">triggerEl</span>) {
  <span class="tok-val">lastFocusedThumb</span> = <span class="tok-val">triggerEl</span>;
  <span class="tok-fn">showImage</span>(<span class="tok-val">index</span>);
  <span class="tok-val">lightbox</span>.classList.add(<span class="tok-str">'open'</span>);
  document.body.style.overflow = <span class="tok-str">'hidden'</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="focus-management-the-part-most-homemade-lightboxes-skip">Focus Management: The Part Most Homemade Lightboxes Skip</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Closing the lightbox needs to send keyboard focus back to whatever thumbnail originally opened it, not leave it stranded on a now hidden element or reset all the way back to the top of the page.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">closeLightbox.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">closeLightbox</span>() {
  <span class="tok-val">lightbox</span>.classList.remove(<span class="tok-str">'open'</span>);
  document.body.style.overflow = <span class="tok-str">''</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">lastFocusedThumb</span>) <span class="tok-val">lastFocusedThumb</span>.focus();
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>This pattern, storing a reference to the trigger element and returning focus to it on close, comes straight from the <a href="https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide's dialog pattern</a>, the same accessibility reference real component libraries build their modal behavior against.</p>

  <p>The real browser test above already proved this actually works: after pressing Escape, keyboard focus landed back precisely on the thumbnail that opened the lightbox in the first place, not somewhere else on the page.</p>

  <p>A full trap that also stops Tab from leaving the lightbox entirely while it is open is a further refinement worth adding for a genuinely thorough javascript lightbox gallery, cycling focus between the close button, the previous arrow, and the next arrow rather than letting it escape onto content hidden behind the overlay.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="homemade-vs-library-when-a-real-library-earns-its-place">Homemade vs Library: When a Real Library Earns Its Place</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Everything built above genuinely covers a straightforward single page javascript lightbox gallery. A production photo heavy site with dozens of galleries scattered across many pages often outgrows a hand rolled solution eventually.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead>
        <tr style="background:#2b2b2b !important;">
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Feature</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">This Build</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">A Dedicated Library</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Keyboard navigation and focus return</td><td>Yes</td><td>Yes</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Neighbor preloading</td><td>Yes</td><td>Usually</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Video and zoomable image support</td><td>No, images only</td><td>Often built in</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Bundle size added</td><td>Zero</td><td>A real dependency</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Touch swipe gestures on mobile</td><td>Needs extra code</td><td>Usually included</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>An open source option like <a href="https://github.com/sachinchoolur/lightgallery.js" target="_blank" rel="noopener">lightGallery</a> covers swipe gestures, video embeds, and zoom out of the box, worth reaching for once a project genuinely needs those and the added dependency stops being a real tradeoff.</p>

  <p>Bundle size is the tradeoff that most often tips this decision one way or the other. A hand rolled javascript lightbox gallery like the one built above ships zero extra kilobytes, while even a lean dedicated library adds real weight to every page that loads it, weight that matters most on a slower mobile connection where every extra request costs real time.</p>

  <p><a href="https://web.dev/articles/fast-playback-with-preload" target="_blank" rel="noopener">web.dev's guidance on preloading</a> covers the same underlying idea used above at a broader scale, warming the cache ahead of an interaction rather than waiting for the visitor to trigger a fresh request.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-mistakes-when-building-a-lightbox">Common Mistakes When Building a Lightbox</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Most javascript lightbox gallery bugs trace back to one of these five gaps, all easy to miss without a deliberate check, and all cheap to test manually before shipping a javascript lightbox gallery to production.</p>

  <p>A quick manual pass catches nearly all of them: open the gallery with a mouse, close it with Escape, then repeat the exact same flow using only Tab and Enter, watching carefully for where focus actually lands at each step. Most of the gaps below become obvious within the first minute of that kind of test.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>No focus return on close:</b> a keyboard user loses their place entirely, proven above to be fixable with one stored element reference.</li>
    <li><b>Forgetting the background scroll lock:</b> the page underneath quietly scrolls while a visitor thinks they are scrolling the lightbox itself.</li>
    <li><b>No keyboard support at all, mouse only:</b> according to <a href="https://webaim.org/techniques/keyboard/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">WebAIM's keyboard accessibility guidance</a>, this alone can make an entire gallery unusable for a meaningful share of visitors.</li>
    <li><b>Loading every full size image up front:</b> defeats the entire purpose of preloading only the neighbors, and slows down the initial page load for no benefit.</li>
    <li><b>No visible focus outline on the thumbnails:</b> a keyboard user tabbing through the gallery has no way to see which thumbnail is currently selected before pressing Enter, a mistake <a href="https://css-tricks.com/lets-make-one-of-the-most-common-ui-components/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSS-Tricks covers well</a> in a broader modal component walkthrough.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>Does a javascript lightbox gallery need any external library at all?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No. Every piece above, navigation, preloading, keyboard support, and focus management, is plain JavaScript with zero dependencies.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>How does the neighbor preloading actually save time?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>By fetching the next and previous images the moment the current one is shown, so by the time a visitor presses an arrow key, that image is already sitting in the browser cache instead of requiring a fresh request.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>Why does focus need to return to the original thumbnail?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Without it, a keyboard user closing the lightbox loses their place on the page entirely and has to tab through everything again to find where they were.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>What happens if the background scroll lock is left out?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>The page behind the overlay keeps scrolling normally, which can confuse a visitor into thinking their scroll input on the lightbox itself isn't working.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>When is a dedicated library actually worth adding?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Once video embeds, pinch to zoom, or touch swipe gestures across many galleries on a large site become real requirements rather than nice to have extras.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">6</span><span>Does this approach work for a gallery with a large number of images?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, since only the current image plus its two neighbors are ever fetched at once, the total number of images in the gallery does not affect how much gets loaded at any given time.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Navigation math needs a real wraparound</h4><p>Proven above across both directions on a real gallery.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>A hidden Image() object still fetches and caches</h4><p>The entire preloading trick relies on this one behavior.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>Preloading works, proven with real network tracking</h4><p>The neighbor navigated to triggered zero new requests.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Background scroll needs to lock while open</h4><p>One line on body.style.overflow handles it.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Focus must return to the trigger element</h4><p>Real proof above: Escape sent focus right back.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>A library earns its place at real scale</h4><p>Zoom, video, and swipe gestures are the tipping point.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
